notes.body: Kōdan Club was a popular monthly magazine of serialized storytelling and historical tales. Nekohachi is reading it for trade, not for study.
notes.span: the *Kōdan Club* he had been buried in

notes.body: A yose is a variety hall for rakugo, mimicry and other acts; a kōza is its raised stage. For Nekohachi the tram has turned into a hall, with the other passengers as his customers.
notes.span: the feeling from the kōza he had just come off

notes.body: Sugamo then held Tokyo's lunatic asylum, by which the tram passed. The joke turns a pun on nest into a slur on the district, then on himself.
notes.span: their tram passing in front of the lunatic hospital

notes.body: Tō Enmei is the Japanese name for the Chinese poet Tao Yuanming, whose famous poem declares his return home from office to the fields. Nekohachi chants the line inwardly as an excuse to want to leave.
notes.span: "let me go home, come—come, let me go home."

notes.body: Sanba is Shikitei Sanba, an Edo comic writer famed for droll, teasing downtown voices. Nekohachi means it as praise from one performer to another.
Konnyaku mondō is a rakugo routine of deliberately mismatched questions and answers that goes nowhere. Nekohachi thinks of it because the critical terms sound to him like pure noise.
notes.span: that konnyaku question-and-answer of the rakugo man

notes.body: The blanks are in the source: circles standing for names of noble houses and viscounts. Leaving them blank is itself good manners about great houses.
notes.span: when I went up to Mr ___ for instance,

data.say: Seven sparse notes for terms, places and allusions the sentences cannot give, with the blanks explained.
